strengths: Significant and useful resource contribution: Amazon Reviews 2023 is a substantially larger and more up-to-date corpus (571M reviews, 48M items, 33 categories, millisecond-precision timestamps, richer metadata) than prior Amazon review datasets, with clear practical value for the community; dataset, code, and checkpoints are released, supporting reproducibility.

The proposed training objective is simple, scalable, and well-motivated: aligning user reviews with item metadata via contrastive learning provides an easily collectable supervision signal for language-item alignment, and the model family (base/large, with MLM-only ablation variants) enables useful analysis.

Evaluation spans multiple tasks (sequential recommendation, conventional product search on ESCI, and a new complex product search task) and multiple domains, with ablations on multi-domain vs. in-domain pretraining and on data curriculum, which supports the generalization claims.

The new complex product search task and the Amazon-C4 benchmark address a genuine gap: keyword-based retrieval (BM25) fails on long, complex natural-language queries, and the task is relevant to LLM-era, language-heavy recommendation scenarios.

Careful experimental hygiene in places: timestamp-based train/val/test splitting to prevent contamination, avoidance of 5-core filtering to reduce distribution shift, and candidate pools spanning all domains.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation bias in the flagship new benchmark: Amazon-C4 queries are ChatGPT rewrites of 5-star reviews of the ground-truth items, i.e., the same (review, metadata) distribution BLAIR is contrastively pretrained on. Even though the test split is held out temporally, BLAIR has a distributional advantage over general-purpose sentence encoders on this benchmark, which weakens the claim that it is a neutral test of language understanding.

Gains over the strongest baseline are modest and inconsistent: SimCSE-Large matches or beats BLAIR-Large on several sequential recommendation metrics (e.g., Beauty R@10/N@10, Baby R@50), and BLAIR-Large sometimes underperforms BLAIR-MLM-Large, muddying the scaling and effectiveness narrative; no statistical significance testing or multiple runs are reported.

Retrieval evaluation setup is weak: NDCG@100 over a candidate pool of only ~51 in-domain plus 50 cross-domain items inflates absolute scores and limits realism; stronger modern dense retrievers (e.g., E5, GTE, BGE, Instructor embeddings) are not compared, only vanilla RoBERTa/SimCSE, making the 'state of the art' framing hard to assess.

Methodological novelty is limited: the approach is a fairly standard contrastive sentence-embedding recipe applied to a new data source; the contribution rests primarily on the dataset and benchmark rather than on technical innovation.

Some reporting gaps and clarity issues: Table 3 lists Beauty/Games/Baby but the text says Beauty/Games/Office; the 'Improvement' row in Table 4 is undefined in its computation; Table 8 conflates BLAIR-MLM with the contrastive model in the multi-domain analysis; the paper is trained on only a 10% downsample due to compute budget, leaving the full-scale results unverified.

Amazon-C4 is LLM-generated (ChatGPT) with no human validation or quality analysis reported (e.g., annotation of relevance, diversity of contexts, failure modes), so the benchmark's quality and long-term utility are not fully established.

strengths: The resource contribution is substantial: AMAZON REVIEWS 2023 is a genuinely large and up-to-date corpus (570M+ reviews, 48M items, 33 categories) with richer metadata and finer-grained timestamps than prior Amazon releases, and it is released publicly along with code and checkpoints, supporting reproducibility and follow-up research.

The proposed complex product search task and the Amazon-C4 benchmark address a real gap: existing product search benchmarks (e.g., ESCI) focus on short keyword queries, and language-heavy item retrieval under long, natural contexts is underexplored.

The evaluation spans multiple tasks (sequential recommendation, conventional search, complex search) and multiple domains, and includes sensible ablations on multi-domain pretraining and data curriculum (Tables 8-9).
Timestamp-based train/test splitting to prevent data contamination is a thoughtful and clearly motivated design choice.

The paper is generally well written and organized, with the training objective, data processing, and implementation details (hyperparameters, hardware, batch sizes) reported at a level that supports reproduction.
weaknesses: The core modeling contribution is thin: BLAIR is a standard RoBERTa-based supervised contrastive model over (review, item metadata) pairs with an auxiliary MLM loss. This pairing idea and objective closely follow prior work (e.g., UniSRec, E-BERT, SimCSE-style training), so the technical novelty beyond 'apply known contrastive training to a bigger, newer dataset' is limited.

The Amazon-C4 evaluation is potentially biased in BLAIR's favor. Queries are ChatGPT rewrites of 5-star user reviews, i.e., the exact (context, item) association BLAIR was contrastively pretrained on. The ground-truth item is the item the source review was written about. The benchmark's distribution thus directly mirrors the pretraining signal, weakening the claim that BLAIR has 'strong generalization' rather than merely matching the benchmark's construction bias. No experiment disentangles this (e.g., human-written complex queries, or queries for held-out items never seen in review-metadata pairs).

The retrieval evaluation protocol is weak: for each query only ~50 randomly sampled in-domain items plus the ground truth form the candidate pool. Ranking among ~51 candidates trivially inflates NDCG@100 and makes the reported gaps hard to interpret relative to realistic full-catalog retrieval over millions of items. Negatives drawn from a different domain could also be separable by superficial signals.

Baseline coverage is inadequate for the retrieval claims. Only BM25, raw RoBERTa, and SimCSE are compared. Strong modern sentence embedders (e.g., E5, GTE, BGE, Instructor) and fine-tuned dense retrievers are absent, so 'best among compared methods' may not mean much for the state of the art.

Results are inconsistent with the narrative. In Table 4, BLAIR-large underperforms SimCSE-large on several metrics (e.g., Beauty R@10/N@10, Baby R@50/N@50), and the sequential recommendation gains are often marginal, yet no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs are reported anywhere.
There is an inconsistency between text and tables: Section 3.2 states experiments cover three domains including Office Products, but Table 4 reports only Beauty, Games, and Baby.
The improvement percentages in Table 4 are ambiguous (relative to which baseline?), and some improvement cells are reported against baselines that were not the strongest in the column.

Missing discussion of limitations and ethics: releasing hundreds of millions of user reviews raises privacy considerations that go unaddressed, and known limitations of the semi-synthetic benchmark construction are not acknowledged.

Only 10% of the collected pretraining data is used, raising the question of whether the dataset's scale was actually exploited, and leaving the resource-contribution and model-contribution claims partially disconnected.

strengths: Significant resource contribution: AMAZON REVIEWS 2023 (570M+ reviews, 48M items across 33 categories) is substantially larger and more recent than prior versions, with finer-grained timestamps and richer metadata, making it broadly useful to the community.

The paper introduces a well-motivated new task (complex product search) and a corresponding evaluation set (Amazon-C4), addressing an underexplored setting between keyword search and conversational recommendation.

Experimental evaluation covers three distinct tasks (sequential recommendation, conventional product search, complex product search) across multiple domains, giving a reasonably broad picture of generalization.
Useful ablations are included: multi-domain vs. in-domain pretraining (Table 8) and data-curriculum strategies (Table 9), which provide insight beyond headline numbers.

Reproducibility practices are good: explicit timestamp-based train/val/test splitting to avoid contamination, released datasets/checkpoints/code, and detailed training hyperparameters, hardware, and data-filtering descriptions.

The motivation is clearly argued: lightweight sentence embeddings that align items with natural language contexts are a practical complement to LLM-based recommenders, and the paper positions itself well against ID-based and text-based alternatives.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in Amazon-C4: queries are ChatGPT rewrites of 5-star user reviews, and BLAIR is pretrained on review-metadata pairs from the same distribution. The model most aligned with the exact training signal is thus evaluated on a test set derived from that very signal, inflating BLAIR's advantage on the paper's flagship task. No independent validation (e.g., human-written complex queries or a different LLM family) is provided.

Limited methodological novelty: the training objective is a standard supervised contrastive loss (SimCSE-style) over review-metadata pairs, closely following prior practice (e.g., Hou et al. 2022 already used reviews as context); the contribution is mostly data at scale rather than a new technique.

Dense retrieval baselines are weak: comparisons are limited to RoBERTa and SimCSE; strong general-purpose embedders (e.g., E5, GTE, Instructor, DPR-style dual encoders trained on large query-document data) are cited but not compared, making it hard to gauge whether the gain comes from recommendation-specific pretraining versus generic sentence-embedding quality.

Mixed and sometimes inconsistent model-scale results: BLAIR-large underperforms SimCSE-large on Beauty (R@10 3.09 vs. 3.90) and BLAIR-MLM-large on several metrics, and the text hedges with 'best on 9 or 12 metrics'; no statistical significance testing or variance reporting is provided for any table.

Evaluation protocol details are thin and may favor the proposed model: e.g., only 50 in-domain negatives per query are added to the candidate pool; the paper's own inconsistency between 'Office' (Section 3.2 text) and 'Baby' (Table 3) as the third sequential-recommendation domain, and Table 4's caption ('Recall@10 and NDCG@10') not matching the reported R@50/N@50 columns, suggests insufficient polish in the experimental reporting.

Pretraining uses only a 10% downsample of the data, so claims about the value of the full 570M-review corpus are not fully substantiated; the abstract's release URL is a placeholder, and the zero-shot claim is not systematically separated from settings where downstream components are trained.

strengths: Substantial resource contribution: the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset (571M reviews, 48M items, cleaner metadata, millisecond timestamps) is a significant community asset that updates the widely used 2018 version, with clear comparative statistics (Tables 1-2).

Comprehensive and well-motivated benchmark design: covering three distinct recommendation scenarios (sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, product search) with appropriate, established downstream architectures (UniSRec, AlphaRec) and controlled downstream parameter counts via adapters, which supports fair comparison across encoders.

Novel and timely subtask: complex-query product search is well motivated by emerging LLM-mediated shopping interfaces, and the dual evaluation strategy (semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 plus real-world Reddit-Movies) thoughtfully addresses the lack of real paired data, with the cross-dataset correlation (r=0.94) providing evidence that semi-synthetic data is a usable proxy.

Strong reproducibility support: a benchmarking toolkit with implementations, data splits, preprocessing details, and evaluation pipelines is released; detailed appendices document hyperparameter search, metadata processing, and candidate-pool construction.

Useful empirical insights beyond the leaderboard: analysis of scaling behavior w.r.t. downstream complexity, adapter design (PCA vs. MRL), metadata richness (title vs. title+description), and an instructive failure case study (Table 11).
Honest limitations section and reasonable ethical discussion of data collection and privacy.
weaknesses: The headline claim that BLAIR and MTEB rankings are uncorrelated rests on a Spearman coefficient of -0.476 with p=0.233 over only 11 models - this is not statistically significant, and with so few points the conclusion 'little correlation' is fragile and risks overinterpretation. More models or bootstrap/significance analysis would be needed.

The Pearson correlation of 0.94 between Amazon-C4 and Reddit-Movies is also computed over just 11 points (and Reddit-Movies has only 1,627 test queries), so the claim that Amazon-C4 is a 'reliable proxy' is underpowered; agreement on model ranking across only two complex-query datasets in different domains may not generalize.

The product search evaluation ranks over a candidate pool of ~51 items (50 sampled in-domain items plus the ground truth) rather than the full corpus, which substantially simplifies the retrieval problem and may inflate NDCG@100 and distort model comparisons relative to realistic full-corpus search.

The scaling-law analysis (Finding 2) is based largely on one model family (Qwen3-Embedding at three sizes) plus a few others, and the discussion in Appendix E is speculative; the evidence for the claimed interaction between encoder scale and downstream complexity is thin.

The semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 queries are generated by ChatGPT rephrasing 5-star reviews with a single prompt; potential stylistic biases, leakage from review content, and sensitivity to the specific LLM/prompt used are not analyzed (e.g., no human validation of query quality).

Item text is restricted to titles only for most Amazon-based tasks based on a small experiment (Section 5.3), which may underestimate the achievable ceiling of semantic encoders and limits the benchmark's coverage of richer metadata despite the dataset's emphasis on cleaner, richer metadata.

The aggregate Borda ranking produces some surprising orderings (e.g., text-embedding-3-large ranked first despite not being best on any per-task average), and sensitivity of conclusions to the aggregation choice is not examined.

The Amazon Reviews 2023 collection pipeline (scraping user identifiers and review pages) is described only at a high level; completeness and sampling biases of the user-centric crawl, and conformance with platform terms, deserve more scrutiny even though the ethics section addresses privacy.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: whether LLM rankings on general-purpose embedding benchmarks (MTEB) transfer to recommendation settings where embeddings serve as frozen semantic features, and the stated motivation (representations consumed by downstream recommenders, short/noisy item text, discriminability requirements) is well articulated.

The evaluation spans three recommendation scenarios (sequential recommendation with UniSRec, collaborative filtering with AlphaRec, and zero-shot product search) across many datasets, with reasonable attempt at controlled comparison via dimension-matching adaptors and parameter-controlled downstream models.

The complex-query product search subtask is a timely idea aligned with emerging conversational shopping interfaces, and the companion real-world Reddit-Movies dataset allows a validation of the semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 as an evaluation proxy (Pearson r=0.94).
The paper reports a benchmarking toolkit, detailed data splits, prompts, and per-dataset results in appendices, which supports reproducibility of the experimental protocol as described.
weaknesses: Serious novelty/attribution problem: the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset described here (571,544,897 reviews, 48,185,153 items, Sep 2023 cutoff) already exists and was released with its own paper (Hou et al., 'Amazon Reviews 2023' / 'Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation', 2024). This manuscript presents it as a new contribution ('We contribute (1) a new large-scale Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset', 'we are the first...') and does not cite the prior release; moreover, the paper's title and acronym BLAIR ('Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation') are verbatim the title of that prior work. This must be resolved — proper attribution and a clear delimitation of what is actually new — before any resubmission can be considered.

The central 'little correlation with MTEB' claim rests on a Spearman correlation over only 11 models (-0.476, p=0.233), which is not statistically significant and is fragile to single-model changes; the claim that MTEB rankings 'do not reflect' recommendation utility is overstated relative to this evidence.

Insight (2) on scaling is internally muddled: the abstract claims performance 'still scales with encoder size', while Section 5.2 reports the trend 'is not consistently observed' and weakens with task complexity; the Qwen3 family results (comparable across 0.6B/4B/8B) undercut the scaling narrative, and the discussion in Appendix E remains speculative hypotheses rather than validated explanations.

The semi-synthetic Amazon-C4 dataset is generated by ChatGPT rephrasing 5-star reviews; both the synthesis quality and potential leakage/coverage biases are not audited (no human validation of rephrased queries, no analysis of entity leakage frequency), weakening the claim that it is a 'reliable proxy'.

Selection of 11 models is biased toward a few families (three Qwen3 variants, several Mistral-based 7B models), so family-level effects may confound the correlation and Borda analyses; the Borda-count ranking over 11 models is a noisy primary criterion and ties/sensitivity analysis are not reported.

Product search uses only 50 in-domain candidates per ground truth plus cross-domain sampling, a highly artificial retrieval setting that makes NDCG@100 values hard to interpret and not comparable to standard search benchmarks.

Only item titles are used as item text; the metadata-analysis (title vs. title+description) experiment is small (3 models, 4 datasets) and its negative result is used to justify dropping richer features, which limits the benchmark's coverage of realistic item text.

Key experimental details needed for verification (e.g., downstream model sizes, training configurations for UniSRec/AlphaRec, variance over seeds) are not reported; results appear single-run without variance estimates, despite small inter-model differences (e.g., 0.0433 vs 0.0434).

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and well-motivated question: whether general-purpose embedding benchmarks (MTEB) are predictive of LLM effectiveness as semantic encoders in recommendation. This is relevant to both the NLP and RecSys communities.

The resource contribution is substantial: a large-scale Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset (570M reviews, 48M items) with cleaned metadata, finer-grained timestamps, and a unified benchmark spanning sequential recommendation, collaborative filtering, and product search.

The new complex-query product search subtask is an interesting addition, with both a semi-synthetic dataset (Amazon-C4, with a reasonable leakage-avoidance design: LLM-rephrased reviews with item names removed) and a real-world dataset (Reddit-Movies), plus a qualitative failure case analysis.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad: 11 embedding models across three size regimes, controlled downstream model parameters via adapters, ablations on metadata choice (title vs. title+description) and adapter design (PCA vs. MRL).
The appendices provide detailed data-splitting, preprocessing, candidate-sampling, and evaluation pipeline descriptions, which support reproducibility in principle.
The qualitative discussion (Appendix E) of why scaling gains weaken in sequentially dependent systems is thoughtful, even if speculative.
weaknesses: Serious novelty/originality concern: the Amazon Reviews 2023 dataset and the 'BLAIR' acronym/benchmark appear to already exist as a public resource from the McAuley lab (Hou et al., 2024, 'Bridging Language and Items for Retrieval and Recommendation', arXiv:2403.03952/KDD'24), yet that work is not cited or differentiated. The paper's claims of contributing a 'new' large-scale dataset and being 'the first to benchmark LLMs for encoding textual features' are therefore not clearly established relative to prior art, and the paper reads as substantially overlapping with that prior release. This must be clarified before the contribution can be assessed.

The headline claim that BLAIR rankings show 'little correlation' with MTEB rests on a Spearman correlation of -0.476 with p=0.233 computed over only 11 models; this is statistically insignificant, and the figure plots only a subset of models. The conclusion that recommendation poses distinct challenges is plausible but overclaimed relative to the evidence.

The scaling-behavior finding is weakly supported: Table 8 shows near-identical results for Qwen3-4B vs. 8B and non-monotonic orderings across models; the 'scaling holds but weakens' narrative is more of a post-hoc interpretation than a demonstrated trend. No significance testing, seed variance, or confidence intervals are reported for any downstream training results.

The claim that Amazon-C4 is a reliable proxy for real-world complex queries is based on a Pearson correlation of 0.94 across 11 mostly-clustered models on a single real-world dataset (Reddit-Movies) with only ~1,627 test queries and a different domain (movies vs. products); the evaluation setups also differ (ranking over ~50 sampled in-domain candidates plus cross-domain items for ESCI/Amazon-C4 vs. a 50k-movie pool for Reddit-Movies), which could confound the correlation.

The semi-synthetic query generation relies on ChatGPT rephrasing with only brief filtering; no human validation of query naturalness or answerability is reported, so data quality of the key new resource is unverified.
The benchmarking toolkit URL is empty in the submitted manuscript ('available at' with no link), which currently undermines reproducibility claims.

Terminology is loose: RoBERTa (~355M) and SimCSE are described as 'LLMs', and some baselines perform near zero on product search (e.g., RoBERTa at 0.0001), raising questions about whether encoding/instruction procedures were fairly applied to weaker models rather than reflecting genuine capability differences.

Only item titles are used as item text for Amazon datasets based on a small-scale experiment (Section 5.3) showing no consistent gain from descriptions; this design choice may underestimate encoders that handle long, noisy text well, which is partly the phenomenon the benchmark intends to measure.
